data.title: The beauty of Slavic jewellery
data.excerpt: Plunge with me into the beauty and uniqueness of Slavic jewellery — the ornaments made and worn chiefly in the times of Great Moravia, among all social classes. Granulation, filigree, repoussé work, chip-carving and inlay produced two spheres of jewellery, the plain and the splendid, from simple ring earrings to the massive pieces of the Veligrad type.
data.metaTitle: The beauty of Slavic jewellery – the art of our ancestors
data.metaDescription: Granulation, filigree, gombíky, temple rings and Veligrad-type earrings: a short tour of the Great Moravian jewellery worn by every social class.

children.text: In today's modern times few people take an interest in history, in ages long past, in their own ancestors, and certainly not in how they dressed, what they wore, what they ate, where they lived; and it occurs to no one how beautiful the jewellery they made was…so…plunge with me into the beauty and uniqueness of Slavic jewellery (since it would not all fit here anyway and you would end up in a muddle)…I shall present to you mainly the jewellery made and worn chiefly in the times of Great Moravia, among the various social classes, mostly from the territory of present-day Slovakia. Just as it is today, in those times too not everyone could “adorn” themselves in the same way. In Great Moravia we can distinguish two spheres of jewellery: the plain and the splendid.

A typical decorative element of Great Moravian jewellery is decoration using granulation and filigree. Decoration by granulation, as the name suggests, is the decoration of the surface of a piece with tiny granules of precious metal. The granules then form various ornaments on the piece. The technique of decorating with fine twisted and notched wires is then called filigree. The wires either form ornaments on the body of the piece (for example on gombíky and belt strap ends), or the piece is made of them alone (basket earrings). On gombíky and various plaques we often meet repoussé decoration. Chip-carving – the cutting of decorative patterns into the surface of an object with deep, sharp cuts. In this way a contrast of light and shade is achieved. Inlay – the hammering of a precious metal into the contrasting metal.

The gombík is a typical piece of jewellery for Great Moravia. It was a dress fastener, or merely an ornament of the dress. They were made of gold, silver, bronze, copper and even of glass. Gombíky made of “ordinary” metals, but also of silver, were often gilded. The decoration of gombíky did not have to be only repoussé; it could also be granulated or in filigree.
Rings decorated with filigree and granulation – of gold or silver, Rings decorated with coloured glass, Rings decorated with stone, Repoussé rings.

The splendid belts of the most prominent magnates were finished with magnificent strap ends. These belt strap ends are a perfect demonstration of the advanced Great Moravian jewellery techniques, using both granulation and filigree. The common people, understandably, could not afford strap ends like these.
Beads for necklaces were most often made of glass. Worked amber and amethyst were also frequently used. From Great Moravia we also know metal beads.

Temple rings took the form of a wire ring, often hammered flat and coiled at one end. The material used was mainly bronze and silver. Temple rings were worn by women tucked into a leather or textile headband.

Like gombíky, Great Moravian earrings are typical of this period and this region. They have a very extensive typology. According to the way they were made we can divide them into earrings made of filigree wire and earrings beaten out of sheet metal. Then there are earrings of the Danubian type, which were often of bronze wire, sometimes decorated with granulation, and of the Veligrad type, which are often very massive and splendid.

Less numerous groups of jewellery are represented by various mounts, fastening brooches, amulets and the like. Lunula-shaped and other pendants come almost exclusively from women's and above all girls' graves. They are often of precious metals and decorated with granulation and filigree, and there are also lunulae cast in bronze.

…this is only a small sample of the incredible beauty of Slavic jewellery; I hope it will touch your heart at least a little, and so I am adding a few more pictures of excavated pieces plus replicas by the very skilful Mr Pavol Francúz, who among other things devotes himself to reconstructions of those Slavic and also other kinds of jewellery.
